dialogue.line: Why do you never call? Your mother misses you. I gave you everything, and this is how you repay me?

jokes.text: Pierce: 'He once sat on me in church just so he could see better.'
jokes.setup: Pierce is explaining why Gilbert deserves the inheritance — he's suffered more under Cornelius.
jokes.punchline: Pierce's chosen evidence is 'He once sat on me in church just so he could see better' — a specific, petty, physical abuse that is so small it becomes enormous. The casualness of the admission reveals Pierce's entire childhood.
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode and one of the best in the season. 'He once sat on me in church just so he could see better' is a masterwork of specificity. The setting (church) makes it worse. The reason (to see better) is so casually practical it's monstrous. The delivery as a throwaway detail in a speech about relative suffering is perfect — Pierce isn't performing pathos, he's just remembering. The specificity implies a lifetime of similar indignities. This is comparable to the Snip Snap anchor in character-specific, escalatory darkness.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: It's actually pronounced 'Crell Moset.' The 'Crell' is silent.

jokes.text: Pierce gives Gilbert his sword to enter the game. Gilbert: 'Oh, Pierce. You really don't know how this works, do you?' Pierce: 'Are you always carrying that?' Jeff (re: the sword): 'Not in the shower.'
jokes.setup: Pierce tries to give Gilbert his in-game sword as a real-world gesture. Gilbert is touched but points out the sword is in the game, not real.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's 'Not in the shower' — implying he does carry it everywhere else — is a quick absurdist kicker after Pierce's confusion about game/reality.
jokes.explanation: Good quick joke. 'Not in the shower' as a deadpan qualifier is the right kind of brief absurdist punctuation. Pierce's confusion is character-consistent. Jeff's line saves the moment from being purely heartfelt.

jokes.text: Gilbert apologizes. The group accepts. Jeff: 'I understand. I have an uncle who makes his own pizza.'
jokes.setup: Gilbert apologizes for his behavior, saying family can make a person do crazy things.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's response — 'I have an uncle who makes his own pizza' — as a parallel to Gilbert's family-driven extreme behavior is a completely disproportionate comparison delivered with utter sincerity.
jokes.explanation: Excellent absurdist non-sequitur. 'I have an uncle who makes his own pizza' as Jeff's example of family making people do crazy things is perfect deadpan — it's so mundane and benign compared to Gilbert's situation that it both trivializes and humanizes the moment. The specificity ('makes his own pizza') makes it funnier than any generic example. This is the kind of joke Community excels at: sincere delivery of an absurd comparison. High quotability.

jokes.text: Gilbert offers to take the group to a bar where they serve a Margarita in a glass 'an entire yard long.' Troy: 'Score.' Pierce: 'This is the greatest day of my life.'
jokes.setup: Gilbert offers to make it up to them with drinks.
jokes.punchline: Troy's one-word 'Score' and Pierce's 'greatest day of my life' in response to a yard-long margarita — both characters' enthusiasm is the joke, particularly Pierce having just given away his inheritance.
jokes.explanation: Pleasant ensemble moment. Pierce's 'greatest day of his life' is ironic given what he's just been through, and also genuinely sweet. Troy's 'Score' is perfect minimalism. Functional character beats.

jokes.text: Pierce to Gilbert: 'Hey, hey, settle a bet. The word "mulatto," is it okay or just borderline?'
jokes.setup: Pierce has just had a touching reconciliation with his new half-brother Gilbert.
jokes.punchline: Pierce immediately ruins the moment by asking Gilbert (his Black half-brother) to adjudicate the acceptability of a racial slur — specifically whether it's 'okay or just borderline,' implying he uses it and just wants calibration.
jokes.explanation: Perfect character payoff after the heartfelt moment. Pierce's question is funny because: (1) the timing is immediately after the reconciliation, (2) asking Gilbert specifically is so wrong it loops back to being right, (3) 'okay or just borderline' implies he's already decided he'll use it and just wants a risk assessment. The group's response — 'We apologize for him. That's okay, he's family.' — is the perfect button.

jokes.text: Group: 'We apologize for him.' Gilbert: 'Oh, that's okay. He's family.'
jokes.setup: Pierce has just asked about a racial slur. The group apologizes.
jokes.punchline: Gilbert accepting the apology — and Pierce's behavior — because 'He's family' closes the episode's emotional arc while also being a funny understatement (family excuses a LOT here).
jokes.explanation: Good button on the Pierce/Gilbert arc. 'He's family' as acceptance of Pierce's racism reframes the entire episode's theme — family is both the source of damage and the thing that excuses it. Works emotionally and comedically.

jokes.text: Post-credits: Abed returns to the game to visit Hilda. 'Hilda, my love, I said I'd come back for you.'
jokes.setup: Episode seems to have ended. Abed returns to the game secretly.
jokes.punchline: Abed returns to his NPC partner with genuine romantic commitment — 'my love' — played completely straight. The joke is that he actually came back.
jokes.explanation: Sweet post-credits tag. Abed's commitment to returning is played sincerely, which is both funny and touching. The 'my love' is a good beat. Rewatch bonus because on the first watch you think the Hilda story ended; this reveals it's ongoing.

jokes.text: Post-credits: Abed and Troy discuss Blorgons vs. Glorbons in alternate universes. Troy: 'A baby. I wasn't expecting this.' Then they pivot immediately to discussing the baby's support needs.
jokes.setup: Abed and Troy are in a sci-fi discussion. A baby appears (Hilda's?). Troy reacts.
jokes.punchline: 'A baby. I wasn't expecting this. Guess we'll have to support it.' Then Troy immediately workshopping his career: 'I could get some kind of job, maybe at Beans and More. I'll probably have to work double shifts.' The speed and sincerity of Troy committing to supporting a pixel baby is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Excellent post-credits bit. Troy instantly and without question accepts responsibility for a pixel baby and starts planning his career at 'Beans and More.' His earnestness is completely in character, and 'Beans and More' as the specific coffee shop is a good detail. The addition of 'I'll probably have to work double shifts, but...' is the right level of pathos for a joke about an NPC baby.

jokes.text: Troy: 'While you're off climbing the ladder at Beans and More, I'll just stay home and raise him alone. That's fine. I'll just give up on my dreams.' Jeff: 'Here we go.' Annie: 'What?' Jeff: 'He needs to learn a strong man can cry.'
jokes.setup: Troy has committed to working at Beans and More for the pixel baby. Then he immediately has second thoughts.
jokes.punchline: Troy escalates to full passive-aggressive martyr speech ('I'll just give up on my dreams'), Jeff recognizes the pattern instantly ('Here we go') and explains Troy's performance ('He needs to learn a strong man can cry') — perfectly deconstructing Troy's emotional arc.
jokes.explanation: Superb post-credits joke. Troy's martyr speech escalating from job commitment to 'I'll just give up on my dreams' is funny because it happens within thirty seconds and is about a pixel baby. Jeff's 'Here we go' is perfect — he's seen this exact Troy spiral before. 'He needs to learn a strong man can cry' is an excellent punchline because it explains Troy's behavior as intentional modeling for the NPC baby, which makes no sense and yet is completely Troy. High character integration for both Jeff and Troy.

jokes.text: "While you're off climbing the ladder at Beans and More, I'll just stay home and raise him alone. That's fine. I'll just give up on my dreams."
jokes.setup: Troy is describing working double shifts at Beans and More to support the baby.
jokes.punchline: Abed immediately responds with passive-aggressive martyrdom — 'I'll just give up on my dreams' — playing the put-upon stay-at-home parent with complete dramatic commitment.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Abed joke. His clinical personality playing 'resentful spouse' is a brilliant character subversion — he's performing a domestic argument trope with complete sincerity. 'I'll just give up on my dreams' as Abed's martyred response is both funny and a perfect window into how he processes human relationship dynamics: through learned scripts.

jokes.text: Post-credits closing: Abed and Troy return to their Blorgons/Glorbons discussion as if nothing happened. 'So, what were you saying about Blorgons? Blorgons... in this other universe, they're actually called Glorbons.'
jokes.setup: After the full emotional arc of the pixel baby crisis, they snap back to their sci-fi discussion.
jokes.punchline: The absolute normalcy of returning to 'Blorgons vs. Glorbons' after everything — and the revelation being so mundane (they're just called something slightly different) — is the perfect absurdist button.
jokes.explanation: Good closing beat. The return to the mundane sci-fi conversation after the domestic crisis is funny in its normalcy. 'They're actually called Glorbons' as the revelation (almost identical names) is an appropriately anti-climactic payoff to the callback.

tmdb_overview: Pierce and his closest friends are summoned to Hawthorne Labs to play a video game that will determine who will inherit his father's fortune.
insight: Video game parody sustains 82 jokes across 44 minutes without relying on standout punchlines.
